data.content_ref: inline:SRC_001 explains why the city is warmer but mis-identifies the single best cross-city predictor of the nocturnal gap. The argument that a geometric sky-view index is the single best predictor is empirically contestable: a large nocturnal-UHI literature identifies anthropogenic heat release as a dominant or stronger cross-city driver (Oke 1973; Sailor 2011), especially in dense high-population cities where nighttime combustion, HVAC rejections, and traffic persist. The target's own commitment surface even includes 'anthropogenic heat' and 'population' as candidate modulators, yet it dismisses them in favor of geometry without quantitative justification. It also concedes a critical countercondition: in a 'sprawling, low-rise city' (i.e., many real-world cities), sky view approaches the countryside and 'radiative trapping cannot explain a large UHI'—an admission that sky-view is not a universally valid single mechanism. By excluding anthropogenic heat as the cross-city modulator while offering no evidence that geometry dominates quantitatively across cities, the target fails to establish the single mechanism the problem demands.
